Consider a parabola. The *parabolic length* of a segment is the length of the projection of this segment on a straight line perpendicular to the axis of symmetry of the parabola. In the parabola, two chords  $AB$  and  $CD$  are drawn, intersecting at the point  $N{}$ . solution_md:
Given the parabola  $y^{2}=2px$  with points  $A(2pa^{2},2pa),B(2pb^{2},2pb),C(2pc^{2},2pc),D(2pd^{2},2pd)$ .

Point  $N(\frac{2p(abc+abd-acd-bcd)}{a+b-c-d},\frac{2p(ab-cd)}{a+b-c-d}\ )$ .

Both products  $(2pa-y_{N})(y_{N}-2pb)=(2pc-y_{N})(y_{N}-2pd)=\frac{4p^{2}(a-c)(a-d)(b-c)(d-b)}{(a+b-c-d)^{2}}$ .

stem_md: Given is a natural number  $n>4$ . There are  $n$  points marked on the plane, no three of which lie on the same line. Vasily draws one by one all the segments connecting pairs of marked points. At each step, drawing the next segment  $S$ , Vasily marks it with the smallest natural number, which hasn't appeared on a drawn segment that has a common end with  $S$ .  Find the maximal value of  $k$ , for which Vasily can act in such a way that he can mark some segment with the number  $k$ ?
solution_md:
Very nice problem, Vasily turns out to be pretty good at drawing segments (well, labeling edges, really). Firstly, consider the obvious graph-theoretic interpretation of the problem:
Vasily has a simple graph $G(V,E)$ with $|V| = n$ and at each step labels an edge $e = \{u,v\}$ the minimal positive integer such that all other edges adjacent to $u$ or $v$ do not have this positive integer as a label. Find the maximal $k$ that Vasily can end up using as a label.
Let $f(n)$ be the maximal $k$ that Vasily can achieve for a given $n \geq 4$ , we will describe $f$ as follows: \[ f(n) = \begin{cases} 2n-4 \text{ even} 2n-3 \text{ odd}. \end{cases} \] For this, we prove the following lemmas. Let $v_1, \cdots, v_n$ be the set of vertices in $G$ . $\textbf{Lemma 1:}$ $f(n) \leq 2n-3$ for all $n \geq 5$ $\textbf{Proof)}$ If Vasily ever writes $t \geq 2n-2$ on an edge $e = \{v_i,v_j\}$ , the other edges $\{v_i,v_k\}, \{v_j,v_l\}$ for $k,l \neq i,j$ of which there are $2n-4$ must contain $1, \cdots, 2n-3$ among them, which is a contradiction. $\blacksquare$ $\textbf{Lemma 2:}$ For $n$ odd, Vasily can indeed achieve $k = 2n-3$ which in turn means that $f(n) = 2n-3$ for $n$ odd. $\textbf{Proof)}$ Isolate vertex $v_1$ and take $G-v_1$ , we have $n-1$ vertices which is even, now assume without loss of generality that the vertices $V-\{v_1\}$ form a regular even-gon. This is in order for us to be able to split the vertices $V-\{v_1\}$ into a set of disjoint perfect matchings. Notice that given this regular polygonal orientation of the vertices, Vasily may label each diameter a certain color $c_i$ for $i \in \{1, \cdots \frac{n-1}{2}\}$ and all other diagonals of $V-\{v_1\}$ perpendicular to this diameter. Then, Vasily firstly picks two of the perfect matchings that create the perimeter of the polygon and then picks each color $c_i$ in order, this then leads to $V-\{v_1\}$ containing each label $1, \cdots, n-2$ exactly $\frac{n-1}{2}$ , more importantly, each vertex in $V-\{v_1\}$ contains each of the aforementioned labels once. Then, picking $\{v_1, v_i\}$ for $i \in \{2, \cdots, n\}$ in order, we must label $\{v_1, v_i\}$ with $n-3+i$ and in fact $\{v_1, v_n\}$ with $n-3+n = 2n-3$ , as desired. $\blacksquare$ $\textbf{Lemma 3:}$ $f(n) \geq 2n-4$ for all even $n \geq 5$ . $\textbf{Proof)}$ We again provide an explicit construction of Vasily's moves. Again construct the same disjoint union of perfect matchings on $V-\{v_1,v_2\}$ as in $\textbf{Lemma 2}$ using the fact that $n-2$ is even, then take $\{v_1, v_i\}$ for $i \geq 3$ which means that $\{v_1,v_i\}$ is labelled with $n-5+i$ for each $i \in \{1, \cdots, n\}$ , then taking $\{v_2, v_i\}$ for $n-1 \geq i \geq 4$ , $\{v_2,v_i\}$ is labelled with $n-6+i$ for all $i \in \{4, \cdots, n-1\}$ , then taking $\{v_2,v_3\}$ , Vasily labels it $2n-6$ . Finally, $\{n-2, \cdots, 2n-6\}$ are the labels on $\{v_2, v_i\}$ for $i \in \{4, \cdots, n-1\}$ and $\{1, \cdots, n-3\} \cup \{2n-5\}$ are the labels of $\{v_j,v_n\}$ for $j \in \{1, 3,4, \cdots, n-1\}$ which means that $\{v_2,v_n\}$ is labeled $2n-4$ , as desired. $\blacksquare$ $\textbf{Lemma 4:}$ $f(n) \leq 2n-4$ for all even $n \geq 5$ . $\textbf{Proof)}$ Assume for the sake of contradiction that $f(n) > 2n-4$ , then clearly $f(n) = 2n-3$ because $f(n) \leq 2n-3$ by $\textbf{Lemma 1}$ . Assume without loss of generality that the largest labelled edge, that is, the edge with label $2n-3$ is the final labelling that Vasily performs on the edge between $\{v_i,v_j\}$ . We have the following "anti claim" to finish off $\textbf{Lemma 4}$ and the problem. $\textbf{Claim:}$ There are disjoint edges adjacent to $v_i$ and $v_j$ labeled $1$ before the edge $\{v_i,v_j\}$ is labeled. $\textbf{Proof)}$ In fact, the set of edges labeled $1$ must form a perfect matching which implies the $\textbf{Claim}$ . Assume for the sake of contradiction otherwise. Firstly, notice that the set of edges labelled $1$ must be a disjoint union of edges, assume that $E-\{v_i,v_j\}$ where we take $E$ to be the set of edges of $K_n$ has $\{v_{a_i},v_{b_i}\}$ as the edges labelled $1$ with $a_i \neq a_j, b_i \neq b_j, a_i \neq b_i$ for $i \neq j \in \{1, \cdots, t\}$ where $t < \frac{n}{2}$ because the set of edges labeled $1$ does not form a perfect matching of $G$ . Then, consider $V - \{a_1,b_1, \cdots, a_t,b_t\}$ whose cardinality is at least $2$ and look at the induced subgraph formed by these vertices. As there are no edges labeled $1$ within these vertices, in fact only $v_i,v_j$ must be remaining, but then, as the last move Vasily would label $\{v_i,v_j\}$ as $1 < 2n-3$ , this is ultimately a contradiction. $\blacksquare$ Now, notice that when Vasily labels $\{v_i,v_j\}$ , by the above Claim, the set of labels adjacent to $v_i$ must be $\{1, x_1, \cdots, x_{n-3}\}$ and labels adjacent to $v_j$ must be $\{1, y_1, \cdots, y_{n-3}\}$ with $x_i \neq x_j, y_i \neq y_j, x_i \neq y_j$ for any $i,j \in \{1, \cdots, n-3\}$ , then $|\{1, x_1, \cdots, x_{n-3}\} \cup \{1, y_1, \cdots, y_{n-3}\}| \leq 2n-5$ which means that the label of $\{v_i, v_j\}$ is at most $2n-4$ , which is a contradiction. $\blacksquare$ Ultimately, $\textbf{Lemma 1, 2}$ prove that $f(n) = 2n-3$ for odd positive integers and $\textbf{Lemma 3,4}$ prove that $f(n) = 2n-4$ for even positive integers. $\blacksquare$
RemarksThe last lemma can clearly be proven without the use of a contradiction, it in fact seems more elegant in that way but in this case establishing the Claim using $1 < 2n-3$ seemed easier, maybe I could have been slightly less lazy and made it work. I think apart from the last part of Lemma 4, the whole problem is pretty motivated, but regardless, it is pretty easy to observe, even without making any progress that the eventual graph must contain labels of $1$ that form a perfect matching for even $n$ , when one makes this connection to something they most likely thought about it early on, they can easily conclude.

stem_md: Initially, a pair of numbers  $(1,1)$  is written on the board.  If for some  $x$  and  $y$  one of the pairs  $(x, y-1)$  and  $(x+y, y+1)$  is written on the board, then you can add the other one. Similarly for  $(x, xy)$  and  $(\frac {1} {x}, y)$ . Prove that for each pair that appears on the board, its first number will be positive.
solution_md: A more generic statement that can be easily proved by induction is that for any  $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$  the expression  $a^2x+aby+b^2$  is strictly positive, where  $(x,y)$  is an arbitrary pair that can ever appear on the board. Substituting  $a=1$  and  $b=0$  gives us the result we need.

Notice that from the pair (a, b) we can move to 3 different pairs:
1.(a+b+1, b+2)
2.(a-b+1, b-2)
3. (1/a, b/a)
Define a quantity for each pair f(a, b) = a - b^2/4
Notice that f(a+b+1, b+2) = f(a, b) = f(a-b+1, b-2), and f(1/a, b/a) = 1/a - b^2/(4a^2) = (a - b^2/4)/a^2 = f(a, b)/a^2. So now we see, that all 3 of these pairs have the same “positives” of the assigned quantity (if the quantity was positive, then it will always stay positive). Because at the start we had f(1, 1) = 3/4.
For every pair (a, b) that we can reach, we have f(a, b) > 0. This means a-b^2/4 > 0 which implies that a >0.

stem_md: Given an infinite sequence of numbers  $a_1, a_2,...$ , in which there are no two equal members.  Segment  $a_i, a_{i+1}, ..., a_{i+m-1}$  of this sequence is called a monotone segment of length  $m$ , if  $a_i < a_{i+1} <...<a_{i+m-1}$  or  $a_i > a_{i+1} >... > a_{i+m-1}$ .  It turned out that for each natural  $k$  the term  $a_k$  is contained in some monotonic segment of length  $k + 1$ . Prove that there exists a natural  $N$  such that the sequence  $a_N , a_{N+1} ,...$  monotonic.
solution_md:
I assume the elements of the sequence are real numbers.

Note that for every positive integer  $k$ , if a segment of length  $k+1$  contains  $a_k$ , then it contains  $a_{k+1}$  as well. Hence  $a_k\ne a_{k+1}$  and the sequence  $b_1,b_2,\ldots\in\{-1,1\}$  defined by  $b_n\doteqdot sign(a_{n+1}-a_n)$  is well-defined. It follows that for each positive integer  $k$ , the element  $b_k$  is contained in a constant segment of length  $k$ . Moreover, it is equivalent to prove that the sequence  $\{b_n\}$  is eventually constant.

The main claim is as follows.**Claim.** Let  $m$  be a positive integer such that  $b_m\ne b_{m+1}$ . Then  $b_1=b_2=\ldots=b_m$ .
*Proof.* As proved above,  $b_m$  is contained in a constant segment of length  $m$ . Since  $b_m\ne b_{m+1}$ , this segment cannot contain  $b_{m+1}$ . Hence this segment must be  $b_1,\ldots,b_m$ .  $\square$ It follows that there is at most one positive integer  $m$  such that  $b_m\ne b_{m+1}$ , so  $\{b_n\}$  is eventually constant.

stem_md: What is the maximal possible number of roots on the interval (0,1) for a polynomial of degree 2022 with integer coefficients and with the leading coefficient equal to 1?
solution_md:
What is the maximal possible number of roots on the interval (0,1) for a polynomial of degree 2022 with integer coefficients and with the leading coefficient equal to 1?
Claim : the greatest number of roots in $(0,1)$ of a monic polynomaial $P(x)\in\mathbb Z[X]$ with degree $n$ is $n-1$ 1) this number is $0$ for all odd $i$ Let $u=\min_{i\in\{0,1,...,n-1\}}|Q(m_i)|$ and positive integer $k>\frac 1u$ Consider $P(x)=x^n+kQ(x)$ . This is monic polynomial $\in\mathbb Z[X]$ Since $|kQ(m_i)|\ge ku>1$ and $m_i^n\in(0,1)$ , we get that $P(m_i)$ has same sign that $Q(m_i)$ And so $P(m_i)<0$ for all even $i$ and $P(m_i)>0$ for all odd $i$ And so at least one real root for $P(x)$ in each interval $(m_i,m_{i+1})$ for any $i\in\{0,1,...,n-2\}$ And so at least $n-1$ real roots in $(0,1)$ And so exactly $n-1$ real roots in $(0,1)$ Q.E.D. Hence answer : $\boxed{2021}$

stem_md: The king assembled 300 wizards and gave them the following challenge. For this challenge, 25 colors can be used, and they are known to the wizards. Each of the wizards receives a hat of one of those 25 colors. If for each color the number of used hats would be written down then all these number would be different, and the wizards know this. Each wizard sees what hat was given to each other wizard but does not see his own hat. Simultaneously each wizard reports the color of his own hat. Is it possible for the wizards to coordinate their actions beforehand so that at least 150 of them would report correctly?
solution_md:
The answer is yes.

We will provide a strategy so that exactly  $150$  wizards will report correctly. Let  $c_0,c_1,\ldots,c_{24}$  be the colors. For  $i=0,1,\ldots,24$ , let  $a_i$  be the number of hats with color  $c_i$ . It is known to the wizards that  $a_0,a_1,\ldots,a_{24}$  are distinct nonnegative integers, hence  $$ 300=\sum_{i=0}^{24}a_i\ge\sum_{i=0}^{24}i=\frac{24\cdot 25}{2}=300. $$  Since equality holds, it follows that  $a_0,a_1,\ldots,a_{24}$  is a permutation of  $0,1,\ldots,24$ . We will show that each wizard has exactly two possibilities of his hat's color, one possibility leads to an even permutation and the other possibility leads to an odd permutation. Consider a wisard  $W$ , and assume he wears a hat with color  $c_p$ , where  $0\le p\le 24$ . Hence  $a_p\ge 1$  and for each  $i=0,1,\ldots,24$ ,  $W$  sees exactly  $a_i$  hats with color  $c_i$  if  $i\ne p$  and also sees  $a_p-1$  hats with color  $c_p$ . There exists a unique integer  $q\in[0,24]$  such that  $a_q=a_p-1$ . In order for  $a_0,a_1,\ldots,a_{24}$  to be distinct, the hat  $W$  wears must be of color  $c_p$  or  $c_q$ . The two guesses differ in a single swap, so they lead to permutations of different parities. 

This way, we can divide the wizards beforehand into two disjoint groups of  $150$  wizards each. The first group will guess an odd permutation and the second group will guess an even permutation. Therefore exactly  $150$  wizards will make a correct guess.
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/International Contests/Kvant Problems/Kvant 2022/2845843.json

candidates:
Here is a different solution, which doesn't give an explicit strategy:

To begin with, note that the minimum possible sum of 25 distinct non-negative integers is 300, which is achieved by adding the numbers from 0 to 24. Therefore, the number of hats of each color must be a permutation of 0 to 24.

We define a state as a configuration of hats that meets the conditions. Let's consider the current state from the perspective of one of the wizards. He can see all hats except for one, so the number of hats of each color he can see must be 1, 2,... k, k, k+1,... 24 for some positive integer k, and he knows that his hat color is one of the two colors that have appeared exactly k times. Therefore, he knows he must be in one of two states.
 
Now let's create a graph, with its vertices being all possible states and two vertices sharing an edge if and only if there is some wizard in one of the states that can confuse it for the other state. Notice that this condition is symmetric for the two vertices and that the degree of each vertex is 300, as every wizard confuses the current state with exactly one other state. When a wizard needs to choose between two states, we can look at the corresponding edge in the graph and direct it toward the state he chooses to believe he is in. Therefore, a strategy for the wizards is equivalent to directing all edges in the graph - each wizard looks at the graph, realizes between which two states he needs to choose, and chooses the state according to how we directed the graph. Furthermore, the number of wizards who guess correctly in a given state is equal to the indegree of this state, i.e. to find a strategy that satisfies the conditions we need to direct the edges in the graph such that each vertex will have an indegree of at least 150. In other words, we need to direct the edges in the graph such that the indegree of each vertex will be greater than or equal to the outdegree. The degrees of all vertices are even so we can take an euler cycle in each connected component and direct the edges according to the cycle. In this way, we get that the indegree of each vertex is equal to its outdegree which is what we wanted.

stem_md: A rock travelled through an n x n board, stepping at each turn to the cell neighbouring the previous one by a side, so that each cell was visited once. stem_md: $m\times n$  grid is tiled by mosaics  $2\times2$  and  $1\times3$  (horizontal and vertical). Prove that the number of ways to choose a  $1\times2$  rectangle (horizontal and vertical) such that one of its cells is tiled by  $2\times2$  mosaic and the other cell is tiled by  $1\times3$  mosaic [horizontal and vertical] is an even number.
solution_md:
Solved with HakNx

Write the number  $1$  in each unit square tiled by  $2 \times 2$  tiles and  $0$  in  $3 \times 1$  tiles respectively. For any possible domino sum up all the numbers on the unit squares covered by that domino and add all the sums together, call this sum  $S$ . Let  $N$  be the number of  $1$ 's on the edges excluding the corners. Double count from each unit squares perspective and notice that  $S \equiv N (mod 2)$ .  
Claim:  $N$  is even. 
Proof: Investigate the 2 cases when  $2 \times 2$  tiles are on the edge but do not contain any corners and the case when a  $2 \times 2$  contains a corner unit square, in each case each  $2 \times 2$  adds exactly  $2$  1's making the total even.  
Now notice that this sum  $S$  is equal to the number of neigboring edges between   $2 \times 2$  's and  $3 \times 1$ 's, which finishes the problem.

stem_md: Given is a graph  $G$  of  $n+1$  vertices, which is constructed as follows: initially there is only one vertex  $v$ , and one a move we can add a vertex and connect it to exactly one among the previous vertices. The vertices have non-negative real weights such that  $v$  has weight  $0$  and each other vertex has a weight not exceeding the avarage weight of its neighbors, increased by  $1$ . Prove that no weight can exceed  $n^2$ .
solution_md:
So, the graph  $G$  is a tree. Take any vertex  $v_0$  and let  $v_1,v_2,\dots,v_d$  be its neighbors. Denote  $\Delta(v_0v_i)=\Delta_i:=w(v_0)-w(v_i)$  where by  $w(v)$  we denote the weight of the vertex  $v$ . The given condition yields  $$ \Delta_1+\Delta_2+\dots+\Delta_d\le d $$  which implies  $$ \Delta_i\le d+\sum_{j\ne i}|\Delta_j|\qquad(1) $$  Let now  $v_0$  be the vertex with  $w(v_0)=0$ . We take it as the root of the tree. It easily follows (starting from the leaves of the tree and using  $(1)$ ) that for any edge  $e=uv, u<v$  we have  $$ \Delta(e)\le \sum_{x>u}d(x) $$  Let  $y$  be any vertex of  $G$  and  $v_0v_1\dots v_i v_{i+1}=y$  be the path from  $v_0$  to  $y$ . We have
\begin{align*}
|w(y)|\le \left|\sum_{j=0}^i\Delta(v_jv_{j+1})\right|&\le \sum_{j=0}^i\sum_{x>v_j}d(x)
&\le \sum_{j=0}^i \left(2|E(T(x_{j+1}))|+1\right)
&\le 2\big((n-1)+(n-2)+\dots+(n-i-1)\big)+(i+1)
&\le (n-1)n+n
&=n^2
\end{align*}
where  $T(x)$  denotes the subtree with root  $x$ . The equality is achieved when  $G$  is a path of length  $n$ .

stem_md:
It is known that among several banknotes of pairwise distinct face values (which are positive integers) there are exactly  $N{}$  fakes. In a single test, a detector determines the sum of the face values of all real banknotes in an arbitrary set we have selected. Prove that by using the detector  $N{}$  times, all fake banknotes can be identified, if a)  $N=2$  and b)  $N=3$ .

*Proposed by S. Tokarev*
solution_md:
Adding to the post above for part (b). 

<details><summary>N=3</summary>Like the previous part, for each query we can deduce the sum of values of counterfeit banknotes in our chosen set by subtracting the total values among our set by the answer returned by the detector (oracle). 

Query 1: select all banknotes, let the sum of of counterfeit banknotes be  $S$ . 

Query 2: select banknotes with values  $v$  with  $\frac{S}{3} < v < S$ ; let  $M$  be the set. Note that there are either 1 or 2 fake banknotes in this range. Let the sum of counterfeit banknotes in this set be  $T$ , so  $\frac{S}{3} <S<T$ . 

Case 1:  $T \le \frac{2S}{3}$ . This means we have one banknote in  $M$  which we know its value,  $T$ . Among the rest, one has value  $< \frac{S - T}{2}$  and one has value  $> \frac{S-T}{2}$ , so Query 3 can just be the set of those with value  $< \frac{S - T}{2}$ . If  $W$  is the answer returned, the answer is now  $(W, S-T-W, T)$ . 

Case 2:  $T > \frac{2S}{3}$ . Let  $U=[0, \frac{S-T}{2})$  and  $V=(\frac{S}{3}, \frac{T}{2})$ . 
Claim: there's exactly one fake banknote in  $U\cup V$ . 

Subcase 2a:  $M$  still consists of a single counterfeit note, this note has value  $T$  (hence  $V$  has no counterfeits), and the other two has values  $< \frac{S - T}{2}$  and  $> \frac{S - T}{2}$  respectively (hence  $U$  has exactly one counterfeit). 

Subcase 2b:  $M$  still consists of two counterfeits with sum  $T$ , i.e. one with  $>\frac T2$  and one with  $< \frac T2$ , meaning  $V$  has one counterfeit. Now the third one has value  $S-T$  hence not in  $U$ . 

Therefore we can let Query 3 be  $U\cup V$ . Let return value be  $W$ . If  $W < \frac S3$ , it has to be subcase 2a, and we know the answer is now  $(W, S-T-W, T)$ . If  $T > \frac S3$ , it has to be subcase 2b and the answer is now  $(S-T, W, T-W)$ .</details>
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/International Contests/Kvant Problems/Kvant 2022/3016091.json

stem_md:
In an infinite arithmetic progression of positive integers there are two integers with the same sum of digits. Will there necessarily be one more integer in the progression with the same sum of digits?

*Proposed by A. Shapovalov*
solution_md:
<details><summary>Answer.</summary>No.</details>

<details><summary>Solution.</summary>Consider the sequence  $3, 1011, \dots$ , where the first two terms have sum of digits 3. The difference 1008 is divisible by 16, so all terms must have remainder 3 modulo 16. We show that a) among those numbers  $16k+3$ , the minimum sum of last 4 digits is 3, and b) there are only two such numbers up to congruence modulo 10000 (i.e.  $0003$  and  $1011$ ). 

Given that such number is odd, if it's sum of last 4 digits is at most 3, then it must end with 1 or 3. In the second case the last 4 digits can only be  $0003$ . In the first case, since it's congruent to 3 mod 4, the tens digits must be odd, so the last two digits can only be  $11$ . Now that the 100s and 1000s digits have to be  $\{0, 1\}$  (while cannot both be 1), we only need to consider  $0011, 0111, 1011$ , and only  $1011$  has remainder 3 modulo 16. This justifies our claim. 

Circling back to the problem, we see that all such numbers in our arithmetic progression with sum of digits = 3 must have the form  $0003$  or  $1011$  in the last 4 digits, and 0 elsewhere, which means there can only be two of them.</details>

stem_md:
Determine all positive integers  $n{}$  and  $m{}$  such that  $m^n=n^{3m}$ .

*Proposed by I. Dorofeev*
solution_md:
Note that  $(m,n)=(1,1)$  is a solution. Moreover,  $m=1\iff n=1$ . So we're left to check the cases where  $m>1$  and  $n>1$ . Now let  $p$  be any prime:
\[
p| n \iff p| m
\]
So  $n$  and  $m$  have the same set of prime factors. Therefore we can write:
\[
n=p_1^{\alpha_1}\dots p_k^{\alpha_k}, m= p_1^{\beta_1}\dots p_k^{\beta_k}
\]
I first prove that  $n\ge 3m$ . Assume otherwise. we have:
\[
p_i ^{n\beta_i}\| m^n, \,
p_i^{3m\alpha_i}\| n^{3m}
\]
Hence:
\[
\forall i \in \{1,\dots,k\} : n\beta_i=3m\alpha_i
\]
Now if  $n < 3m$  then for all  $i$  we have  $\alpha_i < \beta_i$ . This means that  $n|m$  and  $n<m$ . So there's a positive integer  $k>1$  such that  $m=nk$ . So:
\[
(nk)^n=n^{3nk} \iff n^{3k-1}=k
\]
However  $n^{3k-1}\ge 2^{3k-1} > 2^{2k} >k$  which is a contradiction. Hence  $n\ge 3m$ . Therefore for all  $i$ :
\[
\dfrac{\alpha_i}{\beta_i} = \dfrac{n}{3m} \ge 1 \Rightarrow \alpha_i \ge \beta_i
\]
so  $m|n$ . So there's a positive integer  $l$  such that  $n = ml$ . Now:
\[
m^{ml} = (ml)^{3m} \iff m^{l-3} = l^ 3
\]
Obviously, this shows that  $l\ge 3$ . If  $l=3$  then  $1=l^3$  which is in contradiction with  $l\ge 3$ . so  $l$  should be at least  $4$ . For  $l=4$  we have:
\[
m = 4^3 \Rightarrow (m,n) = (64,256)
\]
which is a solution. If  $l = 5$  then  $m^2 = 5^3$  which is a contradiction. So we're left with the cases where  $l\ge 6$ . Note that either  $m$  is a cube or  $l$  is divisible by  $3$ . However if  $m$  is a cube then  $m\ge 8$  and therefore:
\[
m^{l-3} \ge 2^{3(l-3)} \Rightarrow l\ge 2^{l-3} \Rightarrow l \le 5
\]
Which is a contradiction. So  $m$  is not a cube and  $l = 3u$  for some positive integer  $u\ge2$ . Plugging in we get:
\[
m^{u-1} = 3u
\]
Now  $u=2$  yields the solution  $(m,n) = (6,36)$  and  $u=3$  yields the solution  $(m,n) =(3,27)$ . We can simply check that  $u=4$  doesn't give us a solution and finally if  $u\ge 5$  then:
\[
m^{u-1}\ge 2^{u-1} > 3u
\]
which is a contradiction. Hence all the solutions are:
\[
\{(1,1), (3,27), (6,36), (64,256)\}
\]

Let  $n{}$  be a natural number and  $f{}$  be polynomial with integer coefficients. It is known that for any integer  $m{}$  there is an integer  $k{}$  such that  $f(k)-m$  is divisible by  $n{}$ . Prove that there exists a polynomial  $g{}$  with integer coefficients such that  $f(g(m))-m$  is divisible by  $n{}$  for any integer  $m{}$ .

*From the folklore*
solution_md:
<details><summary>solution</summary>Given condition implies that  $f(0), f(1), ..., f(n-1)$  is a complete residue system  $\mod n$ . Thus for any  $0 \le i \le n-1$ , there is  $y_i$  with  $f^{y_i}(i) \equiv i (\mod n)$ . (Graph with vertices  $f(0), f(1),..., f(n-1)$  is union of disjoint cycles)

Let  $K=lcm(y_0,y_1,y_2,...,y_{n-1})$ . Take  $g(x)=f^{K-1}(x)$ .</details>

Let  $f{}$  and  $g{}$  be polynomials with integers coefficients. The leading coefficient of  $g{}$  is equal to 1. It is known that for infinitely many natural numbers  $n{}$  the number  $f(n)$  is divisible by  $g(n)$  . Prove that  $f(n)$  is divisible by  $g(n)$  for all positive integers  $n{}$  such that  $g(n)\neq 0$ .

*From the folklore*
solution_md: Let  $f(n)=q(n)g(n)+r(n)$  with  $deg (r)< deg(g)$ For infinitely many natural numbers  $n$  the number  $r(n)$  is divisible by  $g(n)$   and as   $deg (r)< deg(g)$  then we have that  $\frac{r(n)}{g(n)} \to 0$  so  $r(n)=0$ Condition about leading coefficient is necessary, for example  $f(x)=x(x+1),g(x)=2x$  is contradiction

stem_md:
Find all pairs of natural numbers  $(k, m)$  such that for any natural  $n{}$  the product\[(n+m)(n+2m)\cdots(n+km)\]is divisible by  $k!{}$ .

*Proposed by P. Kozhevnikov*
solution_md:
Really cute  $\nu_p$  problem.

If  $(k!, m)=1$ , take some prime  $p\mid k$  and then  $(p, m)=1$ . We have  $\nu_p(k!)=\sum \lfloor \frac {k} {p^i} \rfloor$  and we have to show  $\nu_p((n+m)(n+2m)\cdots(n+km)) \geq \sum \lfloor \frac {k} {p^i} \rfloor$ . Indeed, among any  $p^i$  consecutive numbers of these there is one multiple of  $p^i$ , so there are at least  $\lfloor \frac {k} {p^i} \rfloor$  multiples of  $p^i$ , done.

If  $p \leq k$  divides  $m$ , take some  $n$  such that  $(n, p)=1$  and thus divisibility is not satisfied for this  $n$ .

stem_md:
In an acute triangle  $ABC$  the heights  $AD, BE$  and  $CF$  intersecting at  $H{}$ . Let  $O{}$  be the circumcenter of the triangle  $ABC$ . The tangents to the circle  $(ABC)$  drawn at  $B{}$  and  $C{}$  intersect at  $T{}$ . Let  $K{}$  and  $L{}$  be symmetric to  $O{}$  with respect to  $AB$  and  $AC$  respectively. The circles  $(DFK)$  and  $(DEL)$  intersect at a point  $P{}$  different from  $D{}$ . Prove that  $P, D$  and  $T{}$  lie on the same line.

*Proposed by Don Luu (Vietnam)*
solution_md:
solutionSuch a crazy geo, I have to spend a whole week to finish this solution.**Claim:** Given an acute triangle $ABC$ . $E,\, F$ lie on $AB,\, AC$ such that $EF \parallel BC$ . Let $D$ be the intersection of $BC$ and the perpendicular bisector of $EF$ ; $S$ be the other intersection of $(DBE)$ and $(DCF)$ . Then $DS$ , $DA$ isogonals wrt the angle $(DE,DF)$ . *Proof.* Let $M$ be the midpoint of $EF$ , $T$ be the point symmetric to $S$ wrt the line $DM$ . Note that, by Miquel's Theorem, we have $S \in (AEF)$ then $T\in (AEF)$ because $T$ and $S$ are symmetric wrt the perpendicular bisector of $EF$ . We have \begin{align*}(TD,\, TA)&\equiv (TD,\, TF) + (TF,\, TA) &\equiv (SE,\, SD) + (EF,\, EA) &\equiv (BE,\, BD) + (BD,\, BE) &\equiv 0 \,\,\,\, (\, mod\, \pi ) \end{align*} Hence $A$ , $T$ , $D$ are collinear. Back to the main problem, denote $S$ be the point symmetric to $T$ wrt the line $BC$ . Let $SK,\, SL$ cut $BC$ at $X,\, Y$ , respectively. $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$ . We have $\frac{ME}{CL}=\frac{CM}{CO}=\frac{TM}{TC}=\frac{SM}{SC}$ and note that $\angle SCL= \angle SME$ so $\triangle SCL \sim \triangle SME$ . Then triangle $SEL$ , $SMC$ must be congruent. Hence, we have: $$ (LE,\, LY) \equiv (LE,\, LS) \equiv (CM,\, CS)\equiv (CT,\, CM)\equiv (DE,\, DY) \,\,\,\, (\, mod\, \pi ) $$ We get that $D,\, E,\, L,\, Y$ are concyclic. Similarly, $D,\, F,\, K,\, X$ are concyclic. Clearly $KL\parallel XY$ and $AD$ is the perpendicular bisector of $KL$ . So by the **Claim** above wrt triangle $SXY$ we get $DS$ , $DP$ isogonals wrt the angle $(DK,DL)$ . But it's easy to see that $DK$ , $DL$ isogonals wrt the angle $(DB,DC)$ Hence, we get $DS$ , $DP$ isogonals wrt the angle $(DB,DC)$ But on the other hand, $DS$ , $DT$ isogonals wrt the angle $(DB,DC)$ So we get $D,\,P,\, T$ are colinear (done).
**Attachments:** [Claim.pdf](https://cdn.artofproblemsolving.com/attachments/4/8/9938a99603c5294b666c094547e22c6d830c92.pdf) [Main.pdf](https://cdn.artofproblemsolving.com/attachments/7/b/9b2e5eb42b6082bf23e56558a5e3b46688406a.pdf)

stem_md:
Does there exist a sequence of natural numbers  $a_1,a_2,\ldots$  such that the number  $a_i+a_j$  has an even number of different prime divisors for any two different natural indices  $i{}$  and  $j{}$ ?

*From the folklore*
solution_md: Yes, there exists. We will construct a sequence with induction. Let  $a_1,a_2$  be the first two elements of this sequence. Suppose that there exists a sequence with length  $k$ , we will show that we can find a  $(k+1).$  number which satisfies the conditions. Take  $a_{k+1}=a_k+(a_1+a_k)^2(a_2+a_k)^2...(a_{k-1}+a_k)^2c$ . Then \[a_i+a_{k+1}=(a_i+a_k)(1+(a_1+a_k)^2...(a_{i-1}+a_k)^2(a_i+a_k)(a_{i+1}+a_k)^2...(a_{k-1}+a_k)^2c)\] $a_i+a_k$  has even number of prime divisors and its prime divisors doesnot divide  $\frac{a_i+a_{k+1}}{a_i+a_k}$ . Denote  $(a_1+a_k)^2...(a_{i-1}+a_k)^2(a_i+a_k)(a_{i+1}+a_k)^2...(a_{k-1}+a_k)^2=p$ . We want  $pc+1$  to have an even number of prime divisors. Suppose that  $ap+1$  has odd number of prime divisors. By Drichlet, we can take a sufficiently large prime  $q\equiv 1(mod \ p)$  and  $b=qa+\frac{q-1}{p}$ . Then,  $pb+1=qap+q=q(ap+1)$  which has an even number of prime divisors since  $(q,ap+1)=1$ . We complete our induction as desired. $\blacksquare$

stem_md:
Call a natural number  $n{}$  *interesting* if any natural number not exceeding  $n{}$  can be represented as the sum of several (possibly one) pairwise distinct positive divisors of  $n{}$ .
[list=a]
[*]Find the largest three-digit interesting number.
[*]Prove that there are arbitrarily large interesting numbers other than the powers of two.
[/list]
*Proposed by N. Agakhanov*
solution_md:
<details><summary>a)</summary>Due to the construction in b) we know that  $992=2^{5}\cdot 31$  is *interesting*. We show that this is the largest three-digit *interesting* integer. Clearly, if  $n$  is *interesting*, then  $n$  must be even (else  $2$  wouldn't have a representation). Note that  $994$ ,  $996$ ,  $998$  are not *interesting* as  $4$ ,  $29$ ,  $4$  don't have a representation, respectively.</details>
<details><summary>b)</summary>We'll show that  $2^{k}n$  is interesting for all odd  $n$  and every  $k\geq \lfloor \log_{2}n\rfloor$  which suffices. Indeed, for any  $m\leq 2^{k}n$ , let  $m=an+b$  where  $0< b\leq n$  and  $0\leq a< 2^{k}$ . Then if  $a=\overline{x_{s}x_{s-1}\dots x_{0}}_{(2)}$  and  $b=\overline{y_{t}y_{t-1}\dots y_{0}}_{(2)}$  are the binary representations of  $a$  and  $b$ : \[m=an+b=n\sum\limits_{i=0}^{s} x_{i}2^{i}+\sum\limits_{i=0}^{t} y_{i}2^{i}=\sum\limits_{i=0}^{s} nx_{i}2^{i}+\sum\limits_{i=0}^{t} y_{i}2^{i}\]
giving the desired representation of  $m$  as a sum of pairwise distinct divisors of  $2^{k}n$ .</details>

stem_md:
Prove that there exists a natural number  $b$  such that for any natural  $n>b$  the sum of the digits of  $n!$  is not less than  $10^{100}$ .

*Proposed by D. Khramtsov*
solution_md:
It suffices to prove that   $$ \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}S(n!)=\infty. $$  Define  $n?=n!/10^{v_5(n!)}$  which is  $n!$  without the final zeros. Now, for any  $t$  we eventually always have  $2^t|n?$  because  $v_2(n!)-v_5(n!)$  grows arbitrarily large. This is because the difference can be written as  $\frac{n-S_2(n)}{2-1}-\frac{n-S_5(n)}{5-1}=\frac{3n}{4}+O(\log(n))$ .
So it now suffices to prove the following lemma: let  $f(t)=\min\{S(x): x\in A_t\}$ , where  $A_t=\{2^tk|k>0 \wedge 5\nmid k\}$ ; then  $\lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}f(t)=\infty$ . Surely  $f$  is weakly increasing because we're taking the minimum of a set with less elements (because  $A_{t+1}\subset A_t$ ). Now, for the sake of contradiction assume that  $f(t)$  is eventually constant. This means that there exists an infinite sequence  $(x_n)_{n\geq N}$  and a constant  $M$  such that  $2^n|x_n$  and  $S(x_n)=M$ . There are infinitely many distinct terms in this sequence because it isn't bounded. So, the infinitely many points of  $\{x_n|n\geq N\}\subseteq A_N$ , all achieve the minimum in the definition of  $f(N)$ . But now, by pigeonhole, take two different terms  $x_m<x_n$  with equal value  $\pmod{10^N}$ . Their common residue  $r\in(0,10^N)$   $\pmod{10^N}$  satisfies  $S(r)\leq S(x_m)=S(x_n)$ . But  $x_n$ , which is bigger than  $x_m$ , must have at least one more nonzero digit than  $r$  to the left, and thus  $S(x_n)>S(r)$ . Now, we know that  $2^N|x_n-q10^N$  for all  $q$ , and in particular  $2^N|r$  (by Euclidean division). This means that the minimum of  $\{S(x)|x\in A_N\}$  couldn't have been  $S(x_n)=S(x_m)$ , since  $S(r)<S(x_n)$ .
Thus, our final result is obtained.

stem_md:
Vasya has  $n{}$  candies of several types, where  $n>145$ . It is known that for any group of at least 145 candies, there is a type of candy which appears exactly 10 times. Find the largest possible value of  $n{}$ .

*Proposed by A. Antropov*
solution_md: The answer is  $160$ . Assume that there exist  $k$  types of candies that appear  $10$  times each. Then,  $10k \leq n$  and, if we remove one candy from each of these  $k$  groups, all the remaining candies don't satisfy the condition, and hence we must have  $n-k<145$  (else we may remove some candies and obtain a non-desirable group of  $145$  candies). Thus, $144 \geq n-k \geq \dfrac{9n}{10},$ and so  $n \leq 160$ . To construct an example of  $160$  candies, just take  $16$  types of candies which appear  $10$  times each. It is easy to check this works.

stem_md:
At a two-round volleyball tournament participated 99 teams. Each played a match at home and a match away. Each team won exactly half of their home matches and exactly half of their away matches. Prove that one of the teams beat another team twice.

*Proposed by M. Antipov*
solution_md: Suppose otherwise, so every pair of teams has a 1-1 record, which means that there were either two home wins or two away wins. Thus the total parity of home wins is even. But by counting over each individual team the number of home wins is  $99\cdot \frac{98}{2}$ , which is odd: contradiction.  $\blacksquare$ **Remark:** If  $99$  is replaced by  $n$ , this problem is true when  $n \equiv 2,3 \pmod{4}$  and false otherwise. An construction for  $n=4$  can be found in **[Worlds 2021 Group D](https://lol.fandom.com/wiki/2021_Season_World_Championship)**.

stem_md:
Given an integer  $h > 1$ . Let's call a positive common fraction (not necessarily irreducible) *good* if the sum of its numerator and denominator is equal to  $h$ . Let's say that a number  $h$  is *remarkable* if every positive common fraction whose denominator is less than  $h$  can be expressed in terms of good fractions (not necessarily various) using the operations of addition and subtraction. 
Prove that  $h$  is remarkable if and only if it is prime.
(Recall that an common fraction has an integer numerator and a natural denominator.)
solution_md:
For the if direction: we construct a way to get  $\frac 1k$  for all  $k <p$ . To start with, we can easily get  $\frac{1}{p - 1}$ . To get  $\frac{1}{p - 2}$ , notice that  $\frac{2}{p - 2} - \frac{2}{p - 1} = \frac{1}{(p-2)(\frac{p - 1}{2})}$ , which wins since the denominator is a multiple of  $p-2$ . To get  $\frac{1}{p - 3}$ , consider the unique number  $0 < x < 3$  with  $3 | p -3 + x$ , then consider  $\frac{3}{p - 3} - \frac{3}{p -3 +  x} = \frac{x}{(p-3)(\frac{p-x}{3})}$ , which can give us  $\frac{x}{p - 3}$ . In general, given that we already have  $\frac{1}{p - i}$  for  $0 < i < k $ , we can always reduce  $\frac{x}{p -k }$  to  $\frac{y}{p - k}$  with  $0 < y < x$ , with  $x | p - k +y$  by considering  $\frac{x}{p - k} - \frac{x}{p - k + y}$ . Thus we can always reduce  $\frac{k}{p -k}$  to  $\frac{1}{p-k}$ . By induction, we are done.

Only if direction: For any prime  $p$  dividing  $h$ , let  $x = \max(v_p(i) \forall i \in [1,h))$ . Then consider a good fraction  $\frac ab$ . Assume to the contrary that this fraction has simplified denominator dividing  $p^x$ . Notice  $v_p(b) \ge x \implies v_p(b) = x \implies v_p(a) \ge 1$ , so this is impossible.

stem_md:
Real numbers are placed at the vertices of an  $n{}$ -gon. On each side, we write the sum of the numbers on its endpoints. For which  $n{}$  is it possible that the numbers on the sides form a permutation of  $1, 2, 3,\ldots , n$ ?

*From the folklore*
solution_md: <details><summary>solution</summary>The solution is all  $n$  with  $n \not \equiv 2 \pmod 4$ . Suppose the sides have  $\sigma(1), \sigma(2), \dots, \sigma(n)$  written on them, starting from some vertex. First of all if  $n$  is odd, then we start by writing  $a$  on the vertex and keep writing  $\sigma(1)-a, \sigma(2)-\sigma(1)+a, \sigma(3)-\sigma(2)+\sigma(1)-a$  along the vertices in a clockwise manner. When we return to  $a$ , due to  $n$  being odd; we get a linear system in  $a$  (fixing the value of  $2a$  and hence  $a$ ). Choosing this  $a$  gives a valid solution, regardless of what  $\sigma$  is. When  $n$  is even, we obtain the same system, except that now the  $a$ s cancel and we obtain that  $\sum_{1 \leq i \leq n} (-1)^i \sigma(i) = 0$ . Working modulo  $2$ , this implies  $4 \mid n$ , for which it is easy to see that solutions exist. A construction is to set  $\sigma(4k+1) = 4k+3, \sigma(4k+2) = 4k+4, \sigma(4k+3) = 4k+2, \sigma(4k+4) = 4k+1$  for all  $0 \leq k < n/4$  and choose  $a = 0$  in the above system. This shows that the numbers  $n$  for which this can be done are precisely  $n \not \equiv 2 \pmod 4$ .</details>

stem_md: Let  $AB$  be a diameter of the circle  $\Omega$  with center  $O{}$ . The points  $C, D, X$  and  $Y{}$  are chosen on  $\Omega$  so that the segments  $CX$  and  $DX$  intersect the segment  $AB$  at points symmetric with respect to  $O{}$ , and  $XY\parallel AB$ . Let the lines  $AB{}$  and  $CD{}$  intersect at the point  $E$ . Prove that the tangent to  $\Omega$  through  $Y{}$  passes through  $E{}$ .
solution_md: Define  $AB\cap CX = F$ ,  $AB\cap DX = G$ ,  $OX \cap \Omega = N$ . Realize that  $-1=(F,G;O,P_{\infty})\overset{X}{=} (C,D;N,Y)$ . Since  $CNDY$  is a harmonic quadrilateral we get that the tangent at  $N$ , the tangent at  $Y$ , and  $CD$  are concurrent, say at  $E'$ . Then since  $\angle{NYX}=90^{\circ}=\angle(NY, AB)$ , it means that  $AB$  is the perpendicular bisector of  $NY$ . Since  $E'$  is the intersection of tangents at  $N$  and  $Y$ ,  $OE'$  is the perpendicular bisector of  $NY$ . Consequently,  $A$ ,  $B$ ,  $O$ , and  $E'$  are collinear. Meaning, the tangent at  $Y$ ,  $CD$ , and  $AB$  are concurrent.  $\blacksquare$

stem_md: Every positive integer greater than  $1000$  is colored in red or blue, such that the product of any two distinct red numbers is blue. Is it possible to happen that no two blue numbers have difference  $1$ ?
solution_md:
Suppose for the sake of contradiction that no two blue numbers have a difference of  $1$ , then for some integer  $n>1000$  such that  $n$  is blue, we have that  $n-1,n+1$  are red so  $n^2-1$  is blue, which means that  $n^2$  is red. 

If  $n^3$  is red then we know that  $n^5$  is blue, so  $n^{10}$  is red, so  $n^{12}$  is blue which means that  $n^{24}$  is red. We also know that  $n^{13}$  is blue, so  $n^{26}$  must be red. However,  $n^{26}=n^{24}n^2$  which are both red, so it must be blue, a contradiction.

Now suppose that  $n^3$  is blue, then  $n^6$  is red. If  $n^4$  is blue, then  $n^8$  is red, so  $n^{11}$  is blue and thus  $n^{22}$  is red. However, we also know that if  $n^8$  is red, then  $n^{10}$  is blue, so  $n^{20}$  is red. This is a contradiction since  $n^{22}=n^{20}n^2$  which are both red. Thus  $n^4$  must be red. Then,  $n^6$  is blue, but since  $n^3$  is blue we must have that  $n^6$  is red. Thus this is a contradiction as well. So the assumption cannot be true.
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/International Contests/Kvant Problems/Kvant 2023/3058622.json

stem_md: In every row of a grid  $100 \times n$  is written a permutation of the numbers  $1,2 \ldots, 100$ . In one move you can choose a row and swap two non-adjacent numbers with difference  $1$ . Find the largest possible  $n$ , such that at any moment, no matter the operations made, no two rows may have the same permutations.
solution_md:
very nice problem**s**olved with Mr Kanav

<details><summary>solution</summary>Make an undirected graph  $G$  on  $100!$  vertices, one for each permutation of  $[100]$  and connect a permutation  $\tau_1$  to a permutation  $\tau_2$  if it is possible to make a move on  $\tau_1$  to convert it into  $\tau_2$  (and vice versa, since the operation is reversible). 

Observe that we simply wish to count the number of connected components of  $G$ . To do this, first to each permutation  $\tau$  we assign the unique string  $S(\tau) = s_1s_2 \dots s_{99}$  of length  $99$ , consisting of characters  $\{<, >\}$  for which the statements: \[\tau_i ~~s_i ~~\tau_{i+1}\] are all true for  $1 \leq i \leq 99$ . 

Claim: If  $u, v$  are connected then  $S(u) = S(v)$ . 

Proof: Suppose we swap numbers  $m, m+1$  to convert  $u \mapsto v$ . Since  $m$  is surrounded by numbers either  $\geq m+2$  or  $\leq m-1$  changing  $m$  to  $m+1$  does not affect  $S(v)$  in that character. Analogously, since  $m+1$  is surrounded by numbers either  $\geq m+2$  or  $\leq m-1$  in this position too,  $S(v)$  remains unchanged. Note that we used the fact that  $m, m+1$  are not adjacent here.  $\square$ It follows that over each connected component of  $G$ , the string  $S(u)$  is fixed. We next show that any two permutations  $\tau_1, \tau_2$  with the same  $S$ -value are in the same connected component. For each string  $s_1s_2\dots s_{99} \in \{<, >\}^{99}$  we assign a permutation  $\tau(s)$  using the following algorithm:


- Step 1: Initialise a variable  $n = 1$ .
- Step 2: Consider the longest string of  $>$  chararcters. Suppose it has length  $m$  (this **may** be zero).
- Step 3: Assign the next  $m+1$  values unassigned to  $\tau$  (in left to right order) the values \[m+n, m+n-1, \dots, n\]
- Step 4: Replace  $n$  with  $n+m+1$ . If  $n \geq 101$ , stop. Otherwise, go to Step 2.
[/list]
It's easy to see that the above algorithm creates a valid permutation with its  $S$ -value being  $s_1s_2 \dots s_{99}$ . 

We now show that each permutation  $\sigma$  of  $[100]$  can be converted to  $\tau\left(S(\sigma)\right)$  after a sequence of operations. Fix any permutation  $\sigma$  and consider doing the following: [list]
- If there are two integers  $m, m+1$  such that  $m+1$  appears before  $m$  in  $\sigma$  and are not adjacent, we swap them.
- Else, we stop.

First, observe that the above cannot go on indefinitely. Indeed, if it did some number in  $[100]$  would move back infinitely often, impossible since there's only  $100$  places it could've been in. Thus we stop at some stage and  $\sigma$  has become some new permuation  $\sigma'$ . 

Claim:  $\sigma' \equiv \tau\left(S(\sigma)\right)$ Proof: We will be inducting. It's a bit finicky to exactly define what we are inducting on now, after all the previous terminology but it will be clear in just a while. Let the location of  $1$  in the permutation  $\sigma'$  be in the  $i$ th position. Now  $2$  is either after  $1$  or before  $1$ . Let us suppose that  $2, 3, \dots, m$  all lie to the left of  $1$  consecutively with  $m$  maximal. We show that  $\sigma'$  starts with  $m$  and thus we may induct down to the permutation after  $1$  by shifting all the values down by  $m$ . Suppose there are numbers before  $m$  and let  $n$  be the smallest among them. Then  $n-1$  lies to the right of the  $[m, \dots, 1]$  block and we could have swapped  $n$  for  $n-1$ ; a contradiction. Thus we can induct down and we prove the claim.

With the two Claims in hand, it is clear that each connected component of  $G$  is described by the string value each vertex has. It follows that the number of connected components of  $G$  is the number of strings in  $\{<, >\}^{99}$ , which is  $2^{99}$  and our final answer.  $\square$</details>

Here is a sketch of my solution. The answer is  $2^{n-1}$ Notice that if one can make several operations that turns one permutation  $\sigma$  into  $\pi$ , one can also turn  $\pi$  into  $\sigma$ , therefore this so called operation actually defines an equivalence relation  $\sim$  on the symmetric group  $S_n$ .
Define a mapping  $\Psi:S_n\to \{+1,-1\}^n$ , for any permutation  $\sigma \in S_n$ ,  $ \Psi (\sigma )=(\textbf{sgn}(\sigma (1)-\sigma(2)),\dots ,\textbf{sgn}(\sigma(n-1)-\sigma (n))$ . The key observation is that the operation does not change the output of  $\Psi$ , i.e. if  $\sigma \sim \pi$ , then  $\Psi(\sigma)=\Psi(\pi)$ , thus there are at least  $2^{n-1}$  equivalence classes.
It is a bit trickier to prove that if two permutations have the same output in  $\Psi$ , they must be equivalent. The answer is  $2^{99}$ . We are clearly being asked to find the number of equivalence classes under the (reversible) operation of repeated swapping.

To prove that there are at least  $2^{99}$  equivalence classes, note that any swap on  $a_1,\ldots,a_{100}$  preserves the values of  $\mathrm{sgn}(a_i-a_{i+1})$  for all  $1 \leq i \leq 99$ . There are  $2^{99}$  possibilities for these values, hence at least this many classes.

To prove that there are at most  $2^{99}$  classes, take an arbitrary permutation and successively perform swaps that decrease its lexicographic order. This eventually terminates, and when this occurs, we must have  $a_i+1 \in \{a_{i-1},a_{i+1},a_{i+2},\ldots,a_{100}\}$  for all  $i$  with  $a_i \neq 100$ . In particular, starting from the end, the sequence should have the form  $k_1,k_1+1,\ldots,100$  for some  $k_1$ . The next term is  $k_2<k_1$ , and then the terms  $k_2,k_2+1,\ldots,k_1-1$  are uniquely determined, and so on. In general we should get (viewing from left to right) an ascending sequence of "down-slopes". It is clear that the choice of ending points on these "down-slopes" uniquely determines them, and there are  $2^{99}$  such choices (since the last term must be an endpoint), so we're done.  $\blacksquare$ For explicitness: if we replace  $100$  by  $6$ , then the permutation formed by choosing endpoints of "down-slopes" at  $2,3,6$  is  $2,1,3,6,5,4$  (formed by constructing in reverse, starting from the end).

stem_md: A square grid  $100 \times 100$  is tiled in two ways - only with dominoes and only with squares  $2 \times 2$ . What is the least number of dominoes that are entirely inside some square  $2 \times 2$ ?
solution_md:
A square grid $100 \times 100$ is tiled in two ways - only with dominoes and only with squares $2 \times 2$ . What is the least number of dominoes that are entirely inside some square $2 \times 2$ ?
Very beautiful. The answer is $100{}$ . For the construction, tile the upper and lower rows with horizontal dominoes and the rest of the board with vertical dominoes; clearly, only those on the upper and lower rows lie entirely in some $2\times 2$ square. Consider the segments of the $100\times 100$ board which do not lie on the boundary of any $2\times 2$ square (as illustrated below, in the case of a $6\times 6$ table) and color them red. Note that a domino lies entirely inside a $2\times 2$ square if and only if it contains a red segment inside it. We also color the boundary of the $100\times 100$ board orange. [asy] size(4.5cm); draw((2,0)--(2,6), gray); draw((4,0)--(4,6), gray); draw((0,2)--(6,2), gray); draw((0,4)--(6,4), gray); draw((1,0)--(1,6), red+linewidth(1.1)); draw((3,0)--(3,6), red+linewidth(1.1)); draw((5,0)--(5,6), red+linewidth(1.1)); draw((0,1)--(6,1), red+linewidth(1.1)); draw((0,3)--(6,3), red+linewidth(1.1)); draw((0,5)--(6,5), red+linewidth(1.1)); draw((0,0)--(0,6)--(6,6)--(6,0)--(0,0), orange+linewidth(1.1)); [/asy] The main observation is the following: if some red and orange segments span a shape of odd area, then that shape cannot be tiled with dominoes, hence a domino must cross its boundary, that is, it contains a red segment inside it (it cannot contain an orange segment inside it, as it would exit the board). Therefore, if we create $100{}$ shapes which have odd areas and disjoint red boundaries, we win! To achieve this, consider all of the $100{}$ squares with odd side-lengths flushed against the upper-left and lower-right corners of the $100\times 100$ board (as illustrated below, in the case of a $6\times 6$ table). This completes the proof. Nice question .Not so easy to explain but I will try.
Lets look at the edges between two adjacent squares. There are  $2n(n-1)$  of them. Call an edge "bad edge" if it lies inside some  $2 \times 2$ .
Every domino contains exactly one edge and if that edge is bad, then that domino lies inside some square  $2 \times 2$ (call it bad domino). So we want to minimize the number of bad dominos.
Paint all the bad edges. They divide the board into: $4$  of  $1 \times 1$  pieces(corner pieces), $196$  of  $1 \times 2$  pieces(edge pieces) and 
some  $2 \times 2 pieces$ (center pieces)

Notice that except for corner pieces each piece's area is even. Starting from a corner piece we will move between pieces by only bad dominos.(We start from a corner piece and the domino that contains that piece is forcefully bad domino. We can say that in the tiling there exist a bad domino that contains only one square of the current piece and that domino leads us to another piece. We can continue this until we reach another corner piece)

So we can find a series of bad dominos that reveals a path between to corner pieces. And actually there are two such path since there are  $4$  corner piece. Since each corner piece is at least  $100$  square apart, each path is at least  $50$  domino length. So there are at least  $100$  bad dominos.

As for example for only  $100$  bad dominos, put  $100$  vertical dominos on the edges and make other dominos horizontal.

We fill in the square at  $i$ -th row and  $j$ -th column by a number   $$ a_{ij}=\begin{cases}j-i-1+(-1)^j&j>i\wedge\frac{j-i}2\not\in\mathbb{Z}i-j-1+(-1)^i&i>j\wedge\frac{i-j}2\not\in\mathbb{Z}1-|i-j|&\frac{j-i}2\in\mathbb{Z}\end{cases} $$  <details><summary>example</summary>when  $100\to 8$  the valuation becomes  $$ \begin{pmatrix}1&1&-1&3&-3&5&-5&71&1&-1&-1&1&-3&3&-5-1&-1&1&1&-1&3&-3&53&-1&1&1&-1&-1&1&-3-3&1&-1&-1&1&1&-1&35&-3&3&-1&1&1&-1&-1-5&3&-3&1&-1&-1&1&17&-5&5&-3&3&-1&1&1\end{pmatrix} $$  the pattern might be clearer if you contemplate it  $2$  by  $2$  at a time</details>
Now if a domino is inside some  $2\times2$  then the sum of its two numbers is  $0$ ;if not, the sum is no greater than  $2$ . Shift the  $2$  by  $2$  boxes so that the top left cell is the bottom right of a box, and instead consider the number of dominoes that occupy two boxes.

Consider a multigraph on the  $51^2$  resulting boxes where there is an edge between two boxes if there is a domino that occupies both. If there are two such dominoes between the same two boxes, there are two edges.

stem_md:
For which maximal  $N$  there exists an  $N$ -digit number with the following property: among any sequence of its consecutive decimal digits some digit is present once only?
	
	Alexey Glebov
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>Let  $f(n)$  be the maximal value of  $N$  if we allow  $n$  distinct digits. So we are looking for  $f(10)$  (we can clearly arrange for the leading digit to be nonzero).
Now, one digit has to occur exactly once in the whole word. Before that digit, there must be a word of  $n-1$  digits, satisfying the condition, hence of length at most  $f(n-1)$ , and the same holds for the word behind that digit. Hence  $f(n) \le 2f(n-1)+1$ .
On the other hand, we can use any construction for  $f(n-1)$  and then create a word of length  $2f(n-1)+1$  by using this word, then the new digit and then again the old word, and it is clear that this will satisfy the condition. Hence in fact  $f(n)=2f(n-1)+1$ .
Since  $f(1)=1$ , it follows easily by induction that  $f(n)=2^n-1$  and in particular  $f(10)=2^{10}-1=1023$ .</details>

stem_md:
We have  $n{}$  coins, one of which is fake, which differs in weight from the real ones and a two-pan scale which works correctly if the weights on the pans are different, but can show any outcome if the weights on the pans are equal. For what  $n{}$  can we determine which coin is fake and whether it is lighter or heavier than the real coins, in at most  $k{}$  weightings?

*Proposed by A. Zaslavsky*
solution_md:
Some observations of mine (not a full sol): $n=1$  and  $n=2$  are obviously impossible for any number of weightings.
<details><summary>Lower bound (probably not tight for all n)</summary>It's easy to see that there are  $2n$  possiblities for which coin is fake and if it's lighter or heavier than real ones ( $n$  coins, and  $2$  possibilities on whether it's lighter or heavier), and each weighting can give us at most  $1$  bit of information (left side is heavier vs. right side is heavier), so we need at least  $\lceil log _2 (2n)\rceil =\lceil log _2 (n)+1\rceil $  weightings.</details>
<details><summary>Sol for powers of 2</summary>Let  $n=2^a$ , for integer  $a>1$ . We will show that we can find the fake coin, and whether it's lighter or heavier than real ones, in  $a+1$  weightings (which is the same as the lower bound). First, denote all coins numbers from  $0$  to  $n-1$ , and write them out in binary. Then, perform  $a$  weightings, where in  $i$ -th weighting, all coins with the  $i$ -th bit set to  $0$  will be on one side of the scale and all remaining coins will be on the other one. Note that because in all of these weightings, the  $2$  pans had an equal number of coins and all coins were on one of the sides, including the fake on, a lighter fake coin would have to be on the lighter in all weightings, and similarly for the heavier one. Now, construct a number  $c$  with  $a$  bits so that  $i$ -th bit is  $0$  iff the side with  $i$ -th bit set to  $0$  was lighter, and  $1$  otherwise. It's easy to see that the only lighter fake coin can be  $c$ , and the only heavier fake coin can be its binary negation (assuming  $a$ -bit numbers). To distinguish these, we make a final weighting, where on one side are  $c$  and its negation and on the other side are  $2$  other coins. By now, we know that one of the coins on the first side is fake and both coins on the other side are real, so the fake coin is lighter iff the side with  $c$  shows as lighter, and that allows us to distinguish between the two possibilities.</details>
I don't have a clue what to do for  $n$ -s which aren't a power of  $2$ . I don't think my lower bound is tight for (at least some of) them (I'm pretty sure  $n=7$  isn't doable in  $4$  weightings).

stem_md: Let  $p{}$  be a prime number. There are  $p{}$  integers  $a_0,\ldots,a_{p-1}$  around a circle. In one move, it is allowed to select some integer  $k{}$  and replace the existing numbers via the operation  $a_i\mapsto a_i-a_{i+k}$  where indices are taken modulo  $p{}.$  Find all pairs of natural numbers  $(m, n)$  with  $n>1$  such that for any initial set of  $p{}$  numbers, after performing any  $m{}$  moves, the resulting  $p{}$  numbers will all be divisible by  $n{}.$ *Proposed by P. Kozhevnikov*
solution_md:
extremely beautiful problem!
solutionThe solution is long and contains many lemmas/claims (pls don't get annoyed, I couldn't find a very clean way to write up this long solution) We show that all such pairs are given precisely by the following two conditions: - $n = p^k$ for some positive integer $k$ . - $m$ is some positive integer strictly greater than $(p-1)k$ . Before we begin, we will need some notation. For a polynomial $P \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ we denote by it's " $p$ -tuple" as the unique collection of integer polynomials \[\{Q_0(x), Q_1(x), \dots Q_{p-1}(x) \}\] with \[P(x) = Q_0(x^p) + Q_1(x^p)x + Q_2(x^p)x^2 + \dots + Q_{p-1}(x^p)x^{p-1}\] It is worth noting that this is **not** the same as base $x^p$ notation. Moreover, we call a polynomial $P$ $n$ -good (for some positive integer $n$ ), if for every polynomial $Q_i$ in its $p$ -tuple we have $n \mid Q_i(1)$ . We first have a very useful lemma. Lemma: Let $P$ be an $n$ -good polynomial and let $R$ denote any arbitrary integer polynoimal. Then $P \cdot R$ is an $n$ -good polynomial. Proof: Let $\{P_0, P_1, \dots, P_{p-1}\}$ and $\{R_0, R_1, \dots, R_{p-1}\}$ denote the $p$ -tuples of $P, R$ respectively. Let $\{Q_0, Q_1, \dots, Q_{p-1}\}$ denote the $p$ -tuple of the product $P \cdot R$ . We note that \[Q_i(x) = \sum \limits_{0 \leq a, b \leq p-1, a+b \equiv i \bmod p} P_a(x) R_b(x)\] In particular, when we evaluate the above at $1$ and read modulo $n$ , every term on the right hand side vanishes, implying $n \mid Q_i(1)$ . Since this holds for any arbitrary $i$ , we deduce that $P \cdot R$ is an $n$ -good polynomial, as required. $\square$ For a circular array $a_0, a_1, \dots, a_{p-1}$ (which we compactly call $a$ from now on) we define $f_k(a)$ as the (circular) array obtained after performing $a_i \mapsto a_i-a_{i+k}$ throughout. We naturally name this process as applying $f_k$ on $a$ . Note that using the operation (or function) $f_k$ on $k$ and $k+p$ yields the same result, thus we may enforce $k \in \{0, 1, \dots, p-1\}$ . Claim: Let $m_1, m_2, \dots, m_k$ be arbitrary integers. Let $b$ be the array obtained after applying (in this order) $f_{m_1}, f_{m_2}, \dots, f_{m_k}$ on some array $a$ . Then for $0 \leq i < p$ we have \[b_i = \sum \limits_{S \subset [1, 2, \dots k]} (-1)^{|S|} a_{i+m(S)}\] where $m(S) = \sum \limits_{v \in S} m_v$ . (yes, this implies that the order in which the operations are performed is irrelevant) Proof: We will prove this by inducting on the number of operations performed. It is clear when $k = 1$ . Now suppose we perform another operation $f_V$ . Then the new value of $b_i$ is given by \[b_i = \sum \limits_{S \subset [1, 2, \dots k]} (-1)^{|S|} a_{i+m(S)} - \sum \limits_{S \subset [1, 2, \dots k]} (-1)^{|S|} a_{i+V+m(S)}\] It is clear that this is exactly equal to the desired value, so we are done with the inductive step. $\square$ In particular, note that the above proves that the $f_i$ commute and that they (and therefore their compositions) are additive. Obviously, note that we can scale as well. We now consider any "good" pair $(m, n)$ , that is, one that satisfies the conditions of the problem. Claim: Let $I$ denote the circular array where one element is $1$ and all others are $0$ s. Then, pair $(m, n)$ is good if and only if when $m$ functions $f_i$ are applied to $I$ we obtain an array which vanishes modulo $n$ (all elements are divisible by $n$ ). Proof: One direction is simple, if $m$ applications of multiple $f_i$ make any array vanish mod $n$ , the same must happen for $I$ . Conversely, suppose that any $m$ functions make $I$ vanish mod $n$ . Let us prove that they must do the same for any circular array $a = \{a_0, \dots, a_{p-1}\}$ . Let $I_0 \equiv I, I_1, I_2, \dots, I_{p-1}$ denote the "circular shifts" of $I$ obtained by rotating exactly $i$ times clockwise, so that the $1$ in $I_i$ is at position $a_i$ . We may write \[a = a_0 I_0 + \dots + a_{p-1} I_{p-1}\] Let $F$ denote an arbitrary composition of $m$ functions $f_i$ . Since $F$ can be scaled and is additive we obtain \[F(a) = a_0F(I_0) + \dots a_{p-1}F(I_{p-1})\] By rotational symmetry, each $F(I_i)$ completely vanishes mod $n$ . In particular, their linear combination $F(a)$ has vanished as well, as required. $\square$ We retain the definition of $I$ above. The next lemma is crucial. Lemma: Let $F$ denote the composition of $m$ functions $f_t$ for some integers $t_1, t_2, \dots, t_m$ . Then $F(I)$ vanishes mod $n$ if and only if the polynomial \[P(x) = (1-x^{t_1})(1-x^{t_2})\dots (1-x^{t_m})\] is $n$ -good. Proof: Let $S$ denote the **multiset** $\{t_1, t_2, \dots, t_m\}$ . Henceforth, when we write $A \subset S$ for a multiset $A$ , we assume that each element of $A$ appears more times in $S$ than it does in $A$ . We let $m(A)$ denote the sum of elements of $m(A)$ . Let $a = F(I)$ . From the claim earlier, we know that for $0 \leq i < p$ \[a_i = \sum \limits_{A \subset S} (-1)^{|S|} a_{i+m(S)}\] Since $a_i \ne 0$ iff $i \ne 0$ and $a_0 = 1$ , we have \[a_i = \sum \limits_{A \subset S, p \mid m(A)+i} (-1)^{|S|}\] Note that \[\sum \limits_{A \subset S} (-1)^{|A|} x^{m(A)} = \prod \limits_{a \in S} (1-x^a) = P(x)\] If we denote by $\{Q_0, Q_1, \dots, Q_{p-1}\}$ as the $p$ -tuple of $P$ , we find that $a_i$ is equal to $Q_{-i}(1)$ . Therefore, for $F(I)$ to vanish fully we require $n \mid Q_{-i}(1)$ for all $i$ . This happens if and only if $P$ is $n$ -good. We make use of $a_i = Q_{-i}(1)$ later as well, so it is worth noting. $\square$ The next claim simplifies the problem quite a lot. Claim: The pair $(m, n)$ is good if and only if the polynomial $(1-x)^m$ is $n$ -good. Proof: First, note that if we select $F = f_1^m$ in the previous lemma, this condition is certainly necessary. Let us quickly show that it is sufficient as well. Suppose we apply $f_v$ with values $v_1, v_2, \dots, v_m$ on $I$ (we showed earlier that we need only consider this array) and it vanishes. This happens if and only if \[(1-x^{v_1})\dots (1-x^{v_m})\] is $n$ -good. If some $v_i = 0$ , that polynomial is the zero polynomial, and it is obviously $n$ -good. If all $v_i \ne 0$ then since $1-x$ divides each $1-x^{v_i}$ we get that $(1-x)^m$ divides that polynomial. But since $(1-x)^m$ is $n$ -good, it follows that the above polynomial is $n$ -good as well, proving the claim. (we proved earlier that all multiples of $n$ -good polynomials are $n$ -good as well) $\square$ The above claim allows us to assume that the only operation we ever perform is $f_1$ (even though we do not enforce this in the discussion that follows). Claim: Let $K$ be any positive integer. Consider applying for each $0 \leq i < p$ the operation $f_i$ on $I$ exactly $K$ times, for a total of $(p-1)K$ operations. Then the final state of $I$ looks like: \[(p^K-p^{K-1}, -p^{K-1}, -p^{K-1}, \dots, -p^{K-1})\] Proof: Write \[P = (1-x)^{K}(1-x^2)^{K} \cdots (1-x^{p-1})^{K} = [(1-x)(1-x^2)\dots(1-x^{p-1})]^K\] and denote its $Q$ -tuple by $\{Q_0, Q_1, \dots, Q_{p-1}\}$ . We first compute $Q_0(1)$ . For this we are going to make use of the so called "roots of unity filter". Let $z= e^{2\pi i/p}$ and note that \[Q_0(1) = \frac{1}{p} \sum \limits_{0 \leq i < p} P(z^i)\] since nonzero coefficients on the other side are the only ones that survive (and exactly $p$ times too). Now, it is easy to compute $P(1) = 0$ and $P(z^i)= p^K$ for all $1 \leq i < p$ . Thus the above sum is exactly $p^{K}-p^{K-1}$ . Now since $P(1) = 0$ , we have \[Q_0(1)+Q_1(1)+\dots+Q_{p-1}(1) = 0\] From the same roots of unity filter, or a bijective argument, we can easily see that $Q_i(1)$ is fixed for $1 \leq i < p$ . Therefore from the above sum we obtain $Q_i(1) = -p^{K-1}$ for all $1 \leq i < p$ . $\square$ Let $(m, n)$ be any good pair. Pick some positive integer $K$ with $K(p-1) \geq m$ and apply those operations (as described above) on $I$ . We applied operations at least $m$ times, so this must have vanished mod $n$ . In particular, $n \mid -p^{K-1}$ . This implies two things. One, $n = p^k$ for some positive integer $k$ , and moreover, \[\left\lceil \frac{m}{p-1} \right\rceil > k\] In other words, \[m \geq k(p-1)+1\] This implies that the conditions mentioned at the start of the solution are necessary for $(m, n)$ to be good. We will now show that they are sufficient as well. Claim: Let $a$ be some array with sum of elements zero. Then it vanishes mod $p$ after applying $f_1$ on $a$ exactly $p-1$ times. Proof: The idea here is a bit obscure. We first find a preimage of $a$ under $f_1$ . Fix $b_{p-1} = 1$ and now backward induct to find each $b_i$ using $b_i = a_i+b_{i+1}$ . Since the sum of elements of $a$ is zero, we ensure that $b_0$ is not wrongly defined twice. Note that $f_1(b) = a$ . We now simply prove that any array $b$ vanishes after applying $f_1$ exactly $p$ times. Let $S = \{1, 1, \dots, 1\}$ , where $|S| = p$ . Suppose the final array is $c$ . From an earlier claim, we have for each $1 \leq i < p$ : \[c_i = \sum \limits_{A \subset S} (-1)^{|A|} b_{i+m(A)} \] Using the simple structure of $S$ , we can simplify the above to \[c_i = \sum \limits_{0 \leq j \leq p} (-1)^j\binom{p}{j} b_{i+j}\] Since $\binom{p}{j}$ is divisible by $p$ for all $j \ne 0, p$ the above reduces (mod $p$ ) to \[c_i = b_i + (-1)^p b_i\] From FLT (yes) we have $(-1)^p \equiv -1 \pmod p$ and so $c_i \equiv b_i-b_i \equiv 0 \pmod p$ . Then, the pair $(m, p^k)$ is good for all $m > (p-1)k$ . Proof: Clearly, it suffices to prove the above for $m = (p-1)k+1$ . Let's start with any array $a$ . Apply the operation $f_1$ on $a$ . @below, here is some motivation behind what I did:
extremely long motivationThe first thing I was thinking about was what $n$ could be. You mainly care about the prime divisors of $n$ and I had conjectured early on that it's most likely powers of $p$ . And since scaling down and repeating that argument gets powers of $p$ too, I wanted to focus on first restricting $n$ to powers of $p$ . This was not easy at first. So I decided to change my tracks a little. The next thing I noticed was that you can express the final term of the $a_i$ s using that subset sum. After some more effort I noticed the $1, 0, \dots, 0$ reduction, despite it being glaringly obvious. Then I noticed that after the sum simplified you're getting something similar to the $p$ -tuple definition. I'd seen something similar before on ELMO 2023 P5, so that kind of thinking definitely helped. I set up the generating polynomial, did some algebra and basically was trying to find sequences of operations for which computing the $Q_i(1)$ was easy. The first one was repeating $f_1$ over and over, which is easy to describe, but a pain to work with, since it doesn't really behave that well. Sure you have a couple of $\binom{k}{i}$ terms, but they are difficult to work with mod $p$ , plus I don't even want mod $p$ , I want exactly the values after a few operations! I got a breakthrough next. I knew the roots of unity filter trick and again, this is from experience, I set $1, 2, \dots, p-1$ to force symmetry and get a lot of those coefficients equal. After this point I was able to quickly compute things very quickly, and was finally able to force $n$ as a power of $p$ , as I'd claimed. Another note that may help: the structure is really similar to the problem where you count subsets of (say) $\{1, 2, \dots, kp\}$ that sum to things divisible by $p$ . I'd infact already gotten the ceil bound at this point, but it would be long before I would realise its usefulness. I was quite satisfied with having $n = p^k$ but the problem was far from over. I went back to the original statement for a while. I realised now (despite already having thought of this earlier) that what I really wanted was $n \mid Q_i(1)$ . I started looking at $n$ -good polynomials, and realised that I just need that random generating polynomial to be $n$ -good. Here, it took me a very long time to that $n$ -good polynomials, when multiplied with other arbitrary polynomials, give $n$ -good polynomials! After this, I realised that I only care about $f_1$ ! This is probably the crux of my solution. The mere fact that you can assume you only ever perform $f_1$ is extremely useful. However, I must confess, I was very lucky to notice this AFTER already having proven $n$ a power of $p$ , and noticing the previous construction, since that's a very easy equality case to prove (or maybe $f_1$ is too, I didn't really try though since it seemed very messy). In particular, had the problem said only $f_1$ , this may have turned a whole lot harder than you'd think. Or maybe not, I don't know. Now, I started making guesses about what $n$ might be. Anyway, after this it was just grinding the details. Proving that everything vanishes after $p$ operations is easy, but the real reduction happens when you realise that when you repeat those $p$ operations, you're technically "already" done with $1$ operation, since the sum of elements is zero. This leads to the obscure idea in one of the claim proofs, where we create a backward sequence and than proceed $p$ times. This can easily be circumvented, but I chose to do this because that's literally how I came up with it. Here I actually returned to the $K(p-1)$ construction, and realised that I had proven the bound already. The problem was now finally solved. I took a sip of water, and wrote up my solution in a very different order than the way I came up with it, introducing technical things earlier. This was a great problem, and is definitely going down in my list of best (oly?) math problems ever. Very happy I was able to solve it, and many congratulations to the author!

stem_md:
The numbers  $2,4,\ldots,2^{100}$  are written on a board. At a move, one may erase the numbers  $a,b$  from the board and replace them with  $ab/(a+b).$  Prove that the last numer on the board will be greater than 1.

*From the folklore*
solution_md:
<details><summary>solution</summary>Let  $S={2,4,8,...,2^{100}}$ . Note that on performing a move, the sum of the reciprocals of the elements of  $S$  is invariant, as  $\frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{b}= \frac{1}{\left (\frac{ab}{a+b} \right)}$ Or, to be more precise, if  $a_i$  represents the  $i$ th element of  $S$  (i.e.  $2^i$ ), starting from  $1$ , then  $\sum_{i=1}^{100}\frac{1}{a_i}$  is constant.

So, the final number that remains after performing the moves  $= \frac{1}{\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{4}+...+\frac{1}{2^{100}}}$ Applying the GP sum formula on the denominator, we get that this big thingie  $= \frac{1}{1-\left (\frac{1}{2} \right)^{100}}>1$ .</details>

stem_md:
The checkered plane is divided into dominoes. What is the maximum  $k{}$  for which it is always possible to choose a  $100\times 100$  checkered square containing at least  $k{}$  whole dominoes?

*Proposed by S. Berlov*
solution_md:
Fairly easy.

Pick  $N\geq 100$  and think about arbitrary  $N\times N$  square  $S$  on plane. Let  $T$  be set of every  $100\times 100$  square completely inside  $S$ . Then  $|T|=(N-99)^2$ . Also call domino  $D$  is **cut** by square  $L$  if  $D$  shares exactly one unit square with  $L$ .

Let set of dominoes that share unit square with  $S$  be  $X$ , and set of dominoes that cut by  $S$  be  $Y$ . Because every domino in  $Y$  has boundary's square of  $S$ ,  $|Y|<4N$ . Since  $2(|X|-|Y|)+|Y|=2|X|-|Y|=N^2$ , it give us  $|X|<N^2/2+2N$ .

Each domino in  $X$  can be cut by at most  $200$  squares in  $T$ . So total number of cuts will be less than  $200(\frac{N^2}{2}+2N)$ . By double counting, this total number is same as sum of 'number of domino cuts' in squares of  $T$  (because every cut dominoes of square in  $T$  is in  $X$ ).

So their average will be less than  $\frac{200(\frac{N^2}{2}+2N)}{(N-99)^2}=\frac{100(N^2+4N)}{(N-99)^2}$ , which is less than 101 for sufficiently large  $N$ . This means if we choose sufficiently large  $N$ , there exist  $100\times 100$  square cuts at most  $100$  dominoes in  $N\times N$  square. Done!

It can be shown easily that if  $100$  is replaced by  $n$ , there exist  $n\times n$  square contains at most  $n$  cut dominoes(having at least  $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$  dominoes inside).

Very nice problem! We will solve the general case, with  $2N{}$  instead of 100. The answer is  $N(2N-1).$  Observe that showing that a  $2N\times 2N$  square contains at least this many whole dominoes is equivalent to showing that at most  $2N{}$  dominoes are pierced by its boundary.

For  $i=1,2,\ldots,2N$  let  $L_i{}$  denote the lattice of  $2N\times 2N{}$  squares, with one of the vertices at  $(i,i).$  For a set of dominoes  $D{}$  and a set of grid-lines  $\mathcal{L}$  we define the domino-density  $\rho_D(\mathcal{L})$  as the ratio between the number of dominoes in  $D{}$  which are pierced by a line in  $\mathcal{L}$  and the total number of dominoes in  $D.$ Suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that the boundary of any  $2N\times 2N$  square of any lattice  $L_i{}$  pierces at least  $2N+1$  dominoes. Consider a large  $2Nt\times 2Nt$  square and let  $D$  be the set of dominoes that *do not* lie entirely outside this square. Since  $|D|=2(Nt)^2+O(t)$  and using our assumption, we get \[1=\sum_{i=1}^{2N}\rho_D(L_i)\geqslant\sum_{i=1}^{2N}\frac{1/2(t-1)^2(2N+1)}{2(Nt)^2+O(t)}=\frac{N(2N+1)(t-1)^2}{2(Nt)^2+O(t)},\]which is a contradiction for large enough  $t.$  Therefore, there exists a  $2N\times 2N$  square whose boundary pierces at most  $2N$  dominoes. To show that one cannot do better than this, consider the brick-tiling of the plane, and we're done.

stem_md:
Let  $k\geqslant 2$  be a natural number. Prove that the natural numbers with an even sum of digits give all the possible residues when divided by  $k{}$ .

*Proposed by P. Kozlov and I. Bogdanov*
solution_md:
not that bad at all
<details><summary>solution</summary>Let  $s(n)$  denote the sum of digits of  $n$ . Let  $0 \leq r< k$  be any residue, and suppose we are trying to find some  $n$  with  $s(n)$  even and  $n \equiv r \pmod k$ .

Pick a positive integer  $m$  with  $2^m > k$  and consider  $N = 10^{2^m}+1$ . We first note that  $\gcd(N, k) = 1$ . Indeed, if some prime  $p$  divides both  $k$  and  $10^{2^m}+1$ , we obtain  $p \leq n < 2^m$  along with  $\text{ord}_{p}(10) = 2^{m+1} \mid p-1$  at the same time, which is clearly impossible. 

Now since  $\gcd(N, k) = 1$ , it follows that there exists some number  $1 \leq c \leq k$  with \[cN \equiv r \pmod k\]
Consider the number  $cN$  now. Since  $c \leq k < 2^m < 10^{2^m}$  we see that  $cN$ 's decimal expansion looks like  $c$ 's decimal expansion, followed by a bunch of zeros, followed by  $c$ 's decimal expansion again.

In particular,  $s(cN) = 2s(c) \equiv 0 \pmod 2$ . Since  $cN \equiv r \pmod k$ , this solves the problem.  $\square$</details>

stem_md:
Let  $n{}$  be a natural number. The playing field for a "Master Sudoku" is composed of the  $n(n+1)/2$  cells located on or below the main diagonal of an  $n\times n$  square. A teacher secretly selects  $n{}$  cells of the playing field and tells his student


- the number of selected cells on each row, and
- that there is one selected cell on each column.
The teacher's selected cells form a Master Sudoku if his student can determine them with the given information. How many Master Sudokus are there?

*Proposed by T. Amdeberkhan, M. Ruby and F. Petrov*
solution_md: A cute problem! Let's number the columns and rows with the numbers  $1,2,...,n$ . I will assume that in the column with the number  $k$ ,there are  $k$  cells are marked in the field, the same for the rows. Let  $f(n)$  be the answer in the problem. Let's see where the cell is selected in column  $n$ . Let's say it is in the row with the number  $k$ . Suppose that one of the selected cells of columns  $n, n-1,..., n-k+1$ , let's say in column  $t$ , is selected not in the  $k$ th row, but in the  $m$ th. Then note that if we select cells  $(n, k), (t, m)\to (t, k), (n, m)$ , then we will get another Sudoku solution, which contradicts the condition. Now, of course, we also know where the cell in column n is selected. Then it is obvious that if we delete columns  $n, n-1, ..., n-k+1$ , we will get Sudoku with a single solution again. In addition, and now we have the only solution, since we know the row in which all the cells are selected. Then in essence we get that  $f(n)=f(n-1)+f(n-2)+... +f(1)+1$ . But easy to see that  $f(1)=1$ , so by induction  $f(n)=2^{n-1}$ .

stem_md:
It is easy to prove that in a right triangle the sum of the radii of the incircle and three excircles is equal to the perimeter. Prove that the opposite statement is also true.

*Proposed by I. Weinstein*
solution_md: Let the triangle have side lengths  $a,b,c$  and semi-perimeter  $s$ . Let  $x=s-a,y=s-b,z=s-c$ . It is well known that the radius of the A-excircle is  $\frac{\sqrt{sxyz}}{x}$  and the inradius is  $\frac{\sqrt{sxyz}}{s}$ . We get   $$ \sqrt{sxyz}[\frac{1}{s}+\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{y}+\frac{1}{z}]=2s=s+x+y+z $$      $$ sxyz[\frac{1}{s^2}|_{cyc}+\frac{1}{xy}|_{sym}]=s^2|_{cyc}+xy|_{sym} $$     $$ (xyz)^2|_{cyc}-s^3xyz|_{cyc}=0 $$     $$ (sx-yz)(sy-xz)(sz-xy)=0 $$   WLOG assume  $sx=yz\rightarrow{x^2+xy+xz=yz}\rightarrow{(y+z)^2=(x+z)^2+(y+z)^2}$  The result easily follows.

The circle  $\omega$  lies inside the circle  $\Omega$  and touches it internally at  $T.$  Let  $XY{}$  be a variable chord of the circle  $\Omega$  touching  $\omega.$  Denote by  $X'$  and  $Y'$  the midpoints of the arcs  $TY{}$  and  $TX{}$  which do not contain  $X{}$  and  $Y{}$  respectively. Prove that all possible lines  $X'Y'$  pass through a fixed point.

*Proposed by F. Petrov*
solution_md:
We first claim that the incenter I of TXY travels along a fixed circle internally tangent to the other two at T. If N is the tangency point of XY and  $\omega$ , and M is the intersection point of TN and (TXY), then TN/TM is fixed by homothety, and by Fact 5, MN*MT = MI^2, so TI/TN is also fixed, which proves the claim.

Since X’Y’ is the perpendicular bisector of TI, it must pass through the center of the circle that is the locus of I, and this is the fixed point.
